prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: In my opening ballot I put B041 (Car and Parrinello) first and B009 only fifth, so I want to say plainly why I now prefer B009 as the configuration to carry forward. Reading the eight ballots, B009 is the one candidate on which every member independently proposes the same two names and no one questions the pairing; it is first or second for five members and in the top three for six. The substance supports that. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid trapping atoms for spectroscopy, and Ye's group turned it into a clock with many-body-aware stability and systematic uncertainty near 1e-18. It is a clearly bounded invention with measured consequences: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the pending redefinition of the second. Independent confirmation across Sr and Yb laboratories is as strong as for anything on this list. From the standpoint of my own field, a clean experimental result that theory can be tested against matters more than the method-versus-discovery label, and here the payoff has been delivered rather than promised. I still think B041 is a strong and arguably overdue proposal, but it has had no support from anyone but me, and I should not mistake my own ranking for merit that the committee has had a chance to test.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B009 is metrology, and part of the physical lineage (the frequency comb in 2005, ion control in 2012) has already been honoured, so some members will ask whether it is a discovery-class advance or the engineering of a better instrument. The credit is also less exclusive than the two names suggest: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB and NIST groups produced decisive accuracy milestones, and a two-name prize necessarily leaves them out. Finally, I was lukewarm myself for a reason that has not gone away: the credited achievement does not open a new scientific question so much as sharpen an existing measurement, whereas B018 and B010 did open new fields. If the committee decides the prize should reward a change in what physicists can think about rather than in what they can measure, B009 would drop.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first and argues that Katori's magic-wavelength invention and Ye's push to 1e-18 form a clean two-name attribution, while disclosing that Ye trained in Hall's laboratory where Kroll spent a research period.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with the maturity argument; I find the Katori-Ye pairing the least contestable on the list. The disclosed link to Hall's laboratory is a historical professional tie rather than a stake, and I think it is correctly handled by disclosure, but the chair should record it. I would add one qualification to Kroll's claim that other groups contributed demonstrations but not the founding idea: that is true for the concept, but the 1e-18 milestones were reached in several laboratories, so the citation should be written around the invention and its realization, not around a record number that may be superseded.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B017 first: aberration-corrected electron optics made sub-angstrom imaging routine, the credit to Rose, Haider and Urban is natural, and it is mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I take the point on maturity and on the fairness of the triple within the supplied names, and I ranked it eighth only reluctantly. My disagreement is about the prize remit and attribution: Olsson herself notes that the STEM corrector work (Krivanek and colleagues) is outside the credited names, and that is not a small gap, since much of the atomic-resolution spectroscopy and magnetic and electronic-structure mapping that I care about came from the STEM instruments. A prize for the TEM corrector alone would carry an attribution problem that a clock prize does not. I also think the committee would need a distinct discovery-level rationale beyond the instrument; the Ruska precedent helps but does not settle it. I do not think B017 is unserious, and I would not object to it as an alternative later.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B018 third and calls it very mature and a clear follow-on to 2016, but flags that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theorists and the 3D topological insulator work sit outside the credited names, creating a fairness problem.
responses.response: I share that concern and it is the main reason I keep B018 as an alternative rather than my first choice. From my own work I can add that the electronic-structure and ARPES confirmation of both 2D and 3D topological materials is as strong as anything in the field, so I do not doubt the physics; what troubles me is that the prediction of HgTe and the 3D materials are not captured, and that a prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would read as incomplete to many. Pearce's view that a defensible prize exists within the exact credited strings is correct, but defensible is a lower bar than the clean attribution that B009 offers.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B052 first as a clear observational discovery of a new window on the universe, while acknowledging that credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the precursor projects could be disputed.
responses.response: I do not dispute that neutrino astronomy is a real discovery, and I can see why an observational result that nature itself delivers is attractive. But my reading of the ballots is that B052 is the most fragile of the first-place candidates on attribution: Pearce, who knows the field best, would credit only Halzen and Karle, Olsson notes the credit is contested and the collaboration is several hundred people, and the origin of the bulk of the flux is unresolved. I would need a firmer answer on whether the prize rewards the 2013 diffuse flux or the source identifications before I could support it, and without that I would rather not rank it above a candidate with a settled two-name split.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B008 (circuit QED) first, openly noting his own field and institutional proximity, and treats the 2025 prize as related but distinct.
responses.response: I appreciate the explicit disclosure of proximity and I think it is the right way to handle it. On substance I agree that circuit QED is a different discovery from the macroscopic tunnelling recognised in 2025, but I rated it sixth because the sequencing worry that Johansson, Lindroth and Mehlig all mention is real, and because credit for the 2004 strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff) and for Nakamura and Devoret is not settled by the three names. I would want that attribution question answered before moving it ahead of a candidate with no such cloud.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats a precision-metrology invention as discovery-class, given the earlier recognition of frequency combs (2005) and ion control (2012).
Whether the best-performing lattice clocks should be credited more broadly than Katori and Ye, which a two-name citation cannot do.

I moved B009 up from my fifth place and B041 from my first place largely on the basis of colleagues' attribution and maturity arguments; I have not verified the historical priority details independently and rely on recall.

Whether a computational-method prize such as B041 would be seen as physics rather than chemistry, given the 1998 chemistry prize for density-functional theory, which I cannot resolve from the ballots.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B009. My profile documents my own field (electronic-structure theory, magnetism), my PhD under Borje Johansson at Uppsala and a period at Los Alamos, none of which links me to Katori, Ye or their groups. I note that I authored work in the electronic-structure area adjacent to B041 and B018 as a field background, which is a reason I treat my own B041 ranking with caution; Kroll's disclosed tie to the Hall laboratory is a colleague's matter, not mine.
